proposals.relationship: Brandon identifies James’s draft reading and intervention on slave resistance as concrete resources in Williams’s development of Capitalism and Slavery.
proposals.evidence_note: Brandon 2017:317–319 and notes 57–71 reports repeated draft reading, the last-minute addition of The Slaves and Slavery, and Williams’s own bibliographical acknowledgment of The Black Jacobins. This is explicitly scholarly mediation through Brandon and his named historical witnesses, not a fresh reading of the original drafts, 1944 bibliographical page 268, James’s book or correspondence. Brandon distinguishes joint Padmore/James political resources, later political divergence and different emphases on enslaved self-activity versus conflicts within the capitalist class. James is a particular contributor, not the sole origin of every Williams thesis or proof of Williams’s Marxist affiliation.
primary_locators: Brandon 2017:317–319, especially 317/n58–59 and 318/n69; actual original publisher PDF318 visually checked

proposals.relationship: As Brandon recounts, James criticized the optimistic forecast for Caribbean development in Williams’s The Negro in the Caribbean while praising its historical analysis and democratic commitment.
proposals.evidence_note: Brandon 2017:325–326 quotes James’s review objecting that the historical account of capitalism’s long operation did not justify a sudden hopeful change in its future behavior. The target is Williams’s 1942 book and its forecast, alongside praise for his history, nationalism and democracy; this is not a direct rejection of the 1944 Capitalism and Slavery or a verdict that all independence projects fail. Brandon’s note 97 identifies James’s W. F. Carlton pseudonym and the 1943 review. Original review and complete 1942 book remain unread; the criticism is explicitly mediated and does not erase the separate constructive scholarly relationship.
